title: What Employees Do Not Tell the Boss
text:
In the early 2000s Frances Milliken, Elizabeth Morrison and Patricia Hewlin of New York University interviewed forty employees from a range of industries about times they had stayed silent at work. Most had full time jobs and some management experience.

The vast majority, around 85 percent, described at least one occasion when they had been aware of an issue or concern at work and had not raised it with their boss. The topics varied: problems with a colleague's or a supervisor's competence, concerns about pay, disagreement with company policies, suggestions for improving processes, and ethical issues.

When asked why they had kept quiet, the most common reason was fear of being seen negatively, for example labeled as a troublemaker or a complainer. Others worried about damaging a relationship, said speaking up would make no difference, feared retaliation, or did not want to embarrass others. Many said their impressions came from how their organization and particular managers had treated people who spoke up before.
lesson: Assume your people know about problems you do not. Ask them directly, and make sure no one is labeled a troublemaker for raising one.
people: Frances Milliken, Elizabeth Morrison, Patricia Hewlin
source: Milliken, F. J., Morrison, E. W., and Hewlin, P. F. (2003). An exploratory study of employee silence: Issues that employees don't communicate upward and why. Journal of Management Studies, 40(6), 1453-1476.
caveat: It was a small interview study, so the percentage is illustrative rather than precise.
